To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

chronic electrical pacing of the developing heart at physiological rate induces preconditioning, which is characterized by a faster recovery of ventricular electromechanical delay and contractility during reoxygenation after a severe hypoxia.
chronic ventricular pacing in ovo at a physiological heart rate in 4-day-old embryonic chick heart improves the postanoxic recovery in vitro.

1) electrical stimulation of the heart in a normoxic environment induces a protection against a subsequent hypoxiareoxygenation; 2) such an effect is selective, as only some functional parameters are improved; and 3) this protection is not related to the ischemic preconditioning mechanism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a noninvasive, nonischemic, nonpharmacological method to protect the heart of the developing embryo from hypoxia.
the study of the mechanisms involved in cardiac preconditioning.
the study of the mechanisms of protection of the myocardium against ischemia and the development of novel therapeutic approaches.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chronic pacing at physiological rate in the chick heart induces a preconditioning-like phenomenon.
chronic pacing of the ventricles at 110% the intrinsic rate in the developing heart induces a nonischemia-dependent cardioprotection against hypoxia-reperfusion injury.
the electrical pacing per se is not the only factor involved in the protective effect observed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the electrical stimulation per-se, and not the myocardial ischemia, is responsible for the protection observed.

the heart is capable of developing a protective response to a chronic electrical stimulation at near physiological rate, which can be used to protect the heart from a subsequent hypoxi-reoxygenation insult.
the electrical pacing of a normoxic heart induces preconditioning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
chronic electrical stimulation can improve the recovery of cardiac function in a normoxic environment.
electrical stimulation of the heart can induce protection against a subsequent ischemia-reperfusion injury.
the electrical pacing of the heart at a near physiological rate is a nonischemia means to increase myocardium tolerance to a subsequent ischemia-reperfusion injury.
